Patient Vignette: "Marcus"

Marcus is a 53-year-old man of Oceania descent, a photographer who has spent decades capturing the world’s most remote and volatile places. He is married, with two adult children. He presents for therapy at the urging of his wife, who has grown increasingly worried about his withdrawal, irritability, and nightmares.

Marcus’s story begins five years ago, on assignment in a war-torn region of the Pacific. He was embedded with a local militia, documenting the aftermath of a skirmish. He was separated from his escort during a mortar attack and taken by a rival faction. For 47 days, he was held captive in a concrete room with no windows, his camera and all possessions confiscated. He was blindfolded, beaten, and repeatedly interrogated about his allegiances. He was given little food or water. He describes the constant, crushing uncertainty: not knowing if he would be killed, if anyone was looking for him, or if he would ever see his family again. He survived by creating a mental map of the room’s sounds—the drip of a pipe, the footsteps of his captors—and by reciting the names of his children over and over.

Since his release, Marcus has not returned to his career. He cannot. The moment he picks up a camera, his hands tremble. The viewfinder, once a window into the world, now feels like a cage. He has sold most of his equipment. His darkroom, once a sanctuary, now sits locked and unused, the chemicals dried and crusted. He tells me that the smell of fixer now makes him nauseous.

In sessions, Marcus is guarded. He speaks in a flat, measured tone, as if narrating someone else’s story. He describes a persistent, low-grade dread that never leaves him. He avoids crowds, loud noises, and any news coverage of conflict. He cannot watch movies with violence. He has become hypervigilant: he always sits with his back to the wall in restaurants, and he scans every room for exits. He has installed multiple locks on his front door, a fact he acknowledges is irrational in his safe suburban home.

His sleep is fractured. He has nightmares two to three times a week, always the same: he is back in the concrete room, blindfolded, hearing footsteps approach. He wakes in a sweat, heart pounding, often screaming. His wife, a nurse, has learned not to touch him when he wakes, as he has flailed and struck her reflexively. He now sleeps in a separate bedroom, a source of deep shame.

Marcus’s emotional landscape is narrow. He describes feeling “numb” most of the time. He cannot feel joy, even when his grandchildren visit. He feels a profound disconnection from his old self—the adventurous, curious photographer who loved the chaos of a new assignment. He says, “That man died in that room.” He has intense guilt over his survival, wondering why he was released when others were not, and he replays the interrogation endlessly, trying to find a moment where he could have been braver.

His marriage is strained. His wife is patient, but she is exhausted. She tells him he is “not here.” He knows this. He cannot explain the chasm between them. He feels like a ghost in his own home. He has not had a drink in three years, but he admits he thinks about alcohol daily, to dull the edge. He has no interest in photography, no hobbies, no social life. He spends most of his time in his garage, tinkering with an old motorcycle engine, a task that requires focus and silence.

Marcus is a man who has lost his narrative. He once told stories through light and shadow. Now, he lives in the shadows of a concrete room. He is not here to get better, he tells me. He is here because his wife asked him to come. He does not believe therapy can undo what was done. He is here to bear witness, perhaps, to a self he no longer recognizes.
